title: [HLR] /do and /copilot-check: move deterministic steps into tested scripts, load rare branches on demand, and cap growth

labels.name: project:hlr
labels.description: High-Level Requirement — captures the WHY before implementation

body:
## Problem

Two skills show the same pattern:
- **`/do`:** `skills/do/SKILL.md` grew from 1,247 words on 16 October to 3,209 after #23, 2.6× in four weeks.
- **`/copilot-check`:** `skills/copilot-check/SKILL.md` grew from 1,713 words when its loop landed in #3 (4 July) to 3,693 after #25, 2.2×.

In both, every PR added words, and almost nothing ever cut any. The size alone isn't the problem: each skill is about 5,000 tokens, a small fraction of a run's transcript. Three things are:

1. **The ratchet.** Each review round finds gaps, and each fix adds a clause. Nothing pushes back.
2. **Defects cluster where a skill specifies mechanical checks.**
   - **`/do`:** QA and the security gate found about 19 defects in #23's roughly 550 new words. About 11 were about spelling out a deterministic check precisely: which remote URLs to resolve, an empty argument to `gh repo view`, how a ref is encoded.
   - **`/copilot-check`:** most of its fix commits since #3 correct how a query or check behaves. Examples: matching Copilot by account id, the guard on empty threads, a failed poll, a failed thread fetch, reading the rubric from the base branch. #25's run found about 15 more of the same kind: a `jq` that dropped a field, `gh pr checks` printing nothing and exiting 1, the check-link regex, the files API's 3,000-file cap.

   A unit test against recorded `gh` output catches these. A review round costs about twenty agent runs and finds them only when it happens to.
3. **Cross-cutting rules are missed when they matter.** `/do`'s step 7 says it "habitually gets missed". New rules also start to interact. For example, recording out-of-scope fixes on the issue now conflicts with keeping a suspected flaw off GitHub until the owner decides, and the lead resolves that silently.

`/copilot-check` is already about a quarter code: 17 inline bash and `jq` blocks, plus inline commands. None of it is tested, and the lead copies each block and fills in `{owner}`, `{repo}`, `{pr}` and `{scratch}` by hand on every run.

## Approach

Sort each skill's content into three kinds, and keep each where it works best:
- **Judgement** stays in prose: `/do`'s path selection, synthesis and when to ask; `/copilot-check`'s clustering, refute-and-scan, the 80/20 decision, fixes and replies.
- **Invariants** (trust, visibility, shell text, no force-push, never auto-merging) stay as a short block that every brief carries.
- **Algorithms** move into scripts with tests. For `/do` that means turning prose into code. For `/copilot-check` it's mostly moving existing blocks into files that take arguments.

Then load the rarely taken branches only when they're triggered, and stop the growth with a budget. `/do` goes first, so the test harness and the habit of recording `gh` output as fixtures are proven before `/copilot-check` reuses them.

**No separate plan.** #24's breakdown comment is the design record. Some decisions cut across both skills and every PR, so the first cut settles them, and the panel reviews them, before anything is built. Otherwise the first script built would set them by accident and everything after would inherit them:
1. **Runtime and dependencies:** Ruby with the standard library only, or a `Gemfile` in `~/.claude`. The scripts run from inside other repositories.
2. **The script contract:** the JSON each script prints, and the exit codes the skills act on: stop, hold, or a reason to ask the owner.
3. **The test harness:** how tests feed recorded `gh` output to the scripts (for example, a `gh` shim on `PATH`), and how those fixtures are recorded and refreshed.
4. **Shared code:** a small shared library for both skills, or each skill self-contained.
5. **Slicing:** how the work splits into PRs or sub-issues.

Each sub-issue's body carries the decisions it relies on, because a sub-issue's own run doesn't read its parent's comments.

This isn't an instruction-capacity fix in the sense of [ADR-005 in ai-software-architect](https://github.com/codenamev/ai-software-architect/blob/main/.architecture/decisions/adrs/ADR-005-llm-instruction-capacity-constraints.md). That ADR's "~150-200 instructions" figure comes, by way of [HumanLayer's post](https://www.humanlayer.dev/blog/writing-a-good-claude-md), from [IFScale](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.11538v1). IFScale measured whether a single generation includes up to 500 keywords, using 2025 models, and its authors say the result may not generalise to other instruction types. What does carry over is in kind:
- errors are mostly omissions;
- earlier instructions get priority;
- Claude models of that time declined gradually rather than holding steady to a threshold.

Every rule therefore has a cost, which is why a budget makes sense even if the number doesn't hold.

## Acceptance criteria

**`/do`**
- [ ] **Pre-flight is a tested script.** `skills/do/bin/preflight` (Ruby, with RSpec, per the global conventions) does the following, then emits JSON and exits non-zero with a reason when the run must stop:
  - parses the issue reference;
  - runs the GraphQL fetch;
  - resolves and checks the remotes (every push URL, the host, forks);
  - makes the slug and validates the branch;
  - decides whether a branch may be resumed;
  - reads the security focus from the base branch.

  `SKILL.md` keeps only the judgement: what to do with each stop reason, and when to ask. The tests use the `gh` behaviours verified live during #21 as fixtures.
- [ ] **Closing and recording are a tested script.** `skills/do/bin/close`, or a subcommand, does the following:
  - works out the `Closes` lines, including whether a sub-issue in another repository is still open and whether its author is trusted;
  - ticks the verified boxes in the ledger and the issue body;
  - reads and writes the local gate file.
- [ ] **Rare branches are loaded on demand.** These move to `skills/do/references/`, each with a one-line trigger in `SKILL.md`, read when the trigger fires:
  - the gate's block, advisory and resume path;
  - resuming;
  - forks and other repositories.
- [ ] **`/do`'s `SKILL.md` is at least 1,000 words shorter, with no change in behaviour.** The QA walk-throughs from #21 (L1–L4) still hold.

**`/copilot-check`** (after `/do`, reusing its harness)
- [ ] **The promotion gate is a tested script, first.** `skills/copilot-check/bin/promote-check` evaluates every condition from GitHub's data and returns a `verdict`: `PROMOTE`, or `HOLD` with every reason. It covers:
  - the rules read from the base branch;
  - convergence on the head;
  - whose PR it is, and whether it comes from a fork;
  - workflow and rule files;
  - checks, by `bucket`;
  - `mergeable`;
  - auto-merge.

  Phase 6 runs it and acts on its verdict. It goes first because #25 added it and it hasn't yet run live.
- [ ] **The other inline blocks are tested scripts.** The skill runs each through `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`, which Claude Code substitutes when the skill loads, so it works inside any repository:
  - setup: resolving the PR, the rubric from the base branch, the high-water-mark query;
  - the thread fetch, to-do selection and guard;
  - selecting threads to resolve;
  - re-requesting Copilot and watching for its review.

  The fixtures cover the behaviours verified live during #12 and #22.
- [ ] **`/copilot-check`'s `SKILL.md` is at least 800 words shorter, with no change in behaviour.** The walk-throughs from #22's QA still hold.

**Both skills**
- [ ] **The scripts' shared convention is documented.** A README under `skills/` gives the runtime, the JSON contract and exit codes, and how tests feed recorded `gh` output, so a future skill follows the same convention.
- [ ] **A word budget per PR, for every skill.** QA reports each PR's net change in a skill's words. An increase over 100 words needs offsetting cuts, or the owner's explicit agreement in the session.
- [ ] **Evaluation is investigated.** Check whether `claude plugin eval` can replay the walk-through scenarios against each skill and check the lead's decisions. Adopt it if so; otherwise record why not.

**Workflow docs** (added with this issue: the guidance on plans no longer matches practice)
- [ ] **The workflow docs say when a plan is warranted.** Two places change:
  - `CLAUDE.md`'s HLR section ("if the work has real design choices, sketch a plan");
  - step 2 of `playbooks/workflow-guide.md`.

  Both say that `/do`'s breakdown comment is the default design record, and that a separate plan is for work spanning several workstreams, or with research to keep. Since #11, no issue here has had a plan of its own. #9's plan took seven follow-up commits, six of them mirroring what its breakdown and PRs already recorded.

## Context

- **`/do`'s growth:** #9 (to 2,085 words), #11, #13, #15, #17 (2,331), #19 (2,665) and #21 (3,209).
- **`/copilot-check`'s growth:** by PR: #3 (1,783), #14 (3,018), #16 (3,380) and #25 (3,693).
- **Considered, not preferred:**
  - **More sub-agent delegation.** Both skills already delegate wherever a fresh context helps. What the lead still holds is mostly work that needs to ask the owner, which sub-agents can't do. Delegating it would move rules into more briefs rather than remove them.
  - **Orchestration as code with the Workflow tool.** It would make control flow deterministic. But its resume works only within a session, while `/do` resumes across sessions from the ledger. Its size guideline is under 10 agents, and `/do`'s panel alone is 8. Whether a workflow can pause to ask the owner is unchecked. Revisit it once the scripts have shrunk the control flow.
